Abel Ferro, the tuner, reached the Pellam Street hall on a snowy Thursday, two days before Lise Marrow's recital. Lise, the town's best young pianist, said the old upright had been sounding wrong all winter, flat in every octave. Nell Ostrand, the hall's manager, had sent for him, and Edith Garvey, the hall's benefactor, had offered the committee the gift of a new piano as soon as a tuner signed her letter calling the old one worn out.

It was Mrs. Garvey who had first noticed the crack, at a committee meeting in March, and she had pointed it out to Nell, to Lise and to Owen Dorran, the caretaker. Abel saw it for the first time now: a hairline split in the board that had opened since the last entry in the notebook of his old teacher, Tobias Rusk. For thirty years Rusk had tuned this piano each spring and autumn, a shade below standard pitch, and Lise had learned on it. Since his death six years ago the committee had kept its money, and the tunings had stopped.

The piano stood where it always had, at the far end from the stove. Abel looked for a broken string, ready to fit a new one, and found every string sound. It had simply sunk, string by string, through six winters, and he brought it back in an afternoon, to Rusk's pitch. Then he took Mrs. Garvey's letter, struck the words 'worn out' from it, and wrote 'six years untuned' in their place.

'Will it be ready for Saturday?' Nell asked. Abel handed her the letter. 'It's ready. Tell the committee it was ready any October they cared to send for me. And tell Mrs. Garvey I'll sign nothing that calls it worn out to clear a space for her gift.' He snapped his case shut and left.

On Saturday Lise went through her whole programme without a sour note on the piano Mrs. Garvey had called worn out. Mrs. Garvey's new piano went to a school in the next town instead. Abel, listening from the back row, heard the low C ring true on the final chord.

passage:
For forty-six summers a carousel turned on Larkmoor common, its twenty-four horses carved in 1912 by Josiah Fenn. When it closed in 1958, the council sold it off piece by piece, and the horses went to families across the valley who bought them for a few shillings each.

Nora Quill had ridden those horses as a girl. In 1991, newly retired from the post office, she found the auction ledger among some council papers, and she bought a county map and a box of index cards for the families she meant to track down. They proved easy to trace, and most agreed to send the horses home. The first horse she brought home had been left under ivy at the end of a garden. After it came horses from a saddler's shop, a school hall, a chapel basement and a hotel lobby in Brannock, until every horse but one was back within the year.

The band organ was another matter. It had spent thirty years in a damp barn, its painted front split and half its pipes gone, and the one firm that still repaired such organs raised its price by half the week Nora wrote to it. For three years she and two retired engineers rebuilt it themselves, pipe by pipe, in her garage. The rest went quickly. A hand-tinted photograph taken in 1923 showed the original colours, a raffle paid for most of the restoration, and the council agreed in one evening that the carousel should stand on the common again.

That left the grey, which Hal Brigg's father had bought at the auction. When Nora asked for it, Hal drove it over himself the next morning. Before the volunteers could unload it, he screwed a small brass plate to its pole, engraved with the words "Brought home by Nora Quill, 1996," and stood aside so the crowd could read it.

The carousel turned again on the common in July 1996, to its own music. Nora spent the afternoon ticking off lot numbers in the ledger as children climbed on.

passage:
For sixteen summers Dr. Hana Vell has counted the sand beetles of Orsk Spit, pale hunters the size of a thumbnail. They spend the day in burrows in the upper dune and cross the dune foot each night to catch sand fleas along the tide line. Every July Vell sets forty pitfall traps along the dune crest. Last July, her student Joel Arkin's first on the spit, the count fell from its usual eight hundred to two hundred and sixty.

Much had changed on the spit that year. Over the winter the park had put up a sand fence along the dune foot, its slats a hand's width apart. A March storm cut into the dune's seaward face, and for two days seawater ran down the broken sand, though the crest and the traps came through it. In May a boardwalk opened, with lamps that switch off at ten, hours before the beetles stir. Visitors soon left it, wearing paths across the north hollow, where the middle traps stand, on their way to the water.

Arkin spent his first week on his knees along the fence, digging at its base for beetles caught against the slats, and found three. Vell went to her notebooks instead. Year after year they put the thickest burrows on the spit in the north hollow, and when she walked it at dawn the new paths had pressed the sand flat over the very patches her notebooks marked.

Arkin mentioned that the park planned to double the boardwalk's length next spring, and asked what she wanted to tell them. Vell spread the spit's map on the table, drew a line around the hollow, then drew a second line well outside the first, and said the park should see the second line before a single new post went in.

At Vell's request the park roped off the north hollow in August. The spit's one earlier drop, in 2013, had recovered only after the park replanted the dune grass; this July the count was already six hundred and ten.
